title: Rules of Engagement
summary: Rules of engagement are the written agreement that defines the boundaries of an authorised security test: which systems and addresses are in scope, when testing may run, which techniques are forbidden, who may be contacted, and what happens if the test causes harm. They convert a vague permission into an auditable authorisation, because a tester with no written scope is indistinguishable from an intruder from both a legal and a network monitoring point of view. In practice they are agreed before the first packet is sent and signed by someone who genuinely owns the systems, and they include emergency stop conditions and a named point of contact on each side. The mistake that causes most trouble is treating them as paperwork, since a scope defined by an out of date spreadsheet, or verbal approval from a manager who does not own the target, has caused real outages and real disputes.

beginner.definition: Rules of engagement are the written rules for an authorised security test. They say which systems may be tested and which must be left alone. They say when testing may happen and which methods are not allowed. Both sides sign them before any work starts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security testing can cause outages or lose data if it goes too far. Without written limits, nobody can prove that the test was allowed. Testers may also be mistaken for attackers by your own monitoring team. Clear rules protect the systems, the testers, and the company. They also give you a way to stop the test quickly.
howItWorks: The client and the testing team agree which systems, addresses, and services are inside the scope.
They agree the time window, so testing does not clash with busy or risky periods.
They list forbidden actions, such as changing data or testing systems that others depend on.
They name a contact on each side and set a code word to stop work immediately.
They agree how findings will be shared, how they are protected, and when they are destroyed.
Both sides sign, and any change to the scope is written down before the work continues.
beginner.example: Imagine a landlord who gives a locksmith permission to test every door in a block of flats. The note says which flats, which hours, and that no lock may be left broken. It also gives a phone number in case something goes wrong. Without that note, the locksmith is just a stranger trying doors. The note is what turns a suspicious act into authorised work.
takeaways: Rules of engagement turn permission into something you can prove.
Scope must come from someone who really owns the systems.
Agree a stop word and a contact before testing starts.

objectives: Explain what rules of engagement are and why a test needs them in writing.
Identify the elements that a scope statement must contain.
Describe why authorisation must come from the owner of the systems.
Explain how a stop condition protects the environment being tested.
Outline how test findings and data are handled and later destroyed.
